passage: At the bus stop outside school in Izmir, Selin asked Nour how the funeral had gone. Nour zipped her coat up to her chin. "It was a stroke," she said. "Ischaemic, left hemisphere. About four in five strokes are that kind. Dede was seventy-nine, so statistically his risk was already high." Her voice was level, like someone reading from a textbook. Selin waited. "They said the ambulance came quickly," Nour went on. "They did everything in the right order. Nobody made a mistake." The bus came. Nour found them two seats and talked about the brain's blood supply until their stop. Selin nodded and didn't argue. That night, a message lit up Selin's phone on her desk: "Dede used to peel oranges for me in one long spiral." A minute later came another: "I can't stop crying." Selin called her straight away.

qa.q: What did Nour say caused her Dede's death?
qa.a: A stroke, ischaemic, in the left hemisphere.

qa.q: Why might reciting stroke facts feel easier to Nour than talking about the funeral?
qa.a: Nour is grieving and overwhelmed, and orderly facts keep the loss at a distance so she can speak without her voice breaking; the message about the oranges shows the sadness was there all along.

qa.q: Which choice of Selin's helped most, and why?
qa.a: Not arguing with the facts on the bus and then calling straight away when the messages came, so Nour wasn't alone when the tears finally arrived.

qa.q: What was the bus ride like for Selin, listening to the facts?
qa.a: Selin was probably unsure how to help, since a question about the funeral got a lecture back, but she chose to stay close and wait.

grounding: A teenager answers a friend's question about her grandfather's funeral with calm stroke facts and statistics, and the tears come only that night.

passage:
In the school library, Sabina had three printouts spread across the table: kidney function, dialysis, survival rates for people over seventy. Bhupen sat down with his maths book. "Aren't you on leave this week?"
"Came back early." She tapped a chart. "Nani's creatinine was rising for two years. It's a waste product. When the kidneys fail, it builds up." Her voice was the one she used for quiz club.
"Sabina, I'm really sorry about your Nani."
"Thanks. Did you know most people on dialysis in that age group..." She found the line with her finger and read it out, flat and exact.
Bhupen didn't know what to say, so he stayed. At the bell, she stacked the pages neatly. At the gate, she opened her bag and saw Nani's old blue umbrella folded inside. She stood very still, and her eyes filled. Bhupen waited beside her until her father's scooter pulled up.

qa.q: What were Sabina's three printouts about?
qa.a: Kidney function, dialysis, and survival rates for people over seventy.

qa.q: Why does Sabina seem to feel safer talking about creatinine than about her Nani?
qa.a: Explaining the illness keeps the loss at arm's length and uses her steady quiz-club voice; the grief only breaks through when she sees Nani's umbrella.

qa.q: Which choice of Bhupen's helped most, and why?
qa.a: Staying beside her without pushing, so she wasn't alone when the umbrella finally brought the sadness through.

qa.q: How might Sabina's quiz-club tone come across to classmates who don't know her well?
qa.a: They might think she doesn't care about her Nani, when the flat facts are really a way of holding the pain back for now.

grounding: A teenager whose Nani has died talks about kidney failure in a flat quiz voice in the school library, and her grief surfaces only later at the gate.

passage:
Hi Vidya,
You asked how I'm doing since Thatha died. I've been reading a lot. His heart failure was the kind where the left side stops pumping properly. The heart gets bigger to make up for it, which sounds good but isn't. Many people with his condition live around five years after diagnosis, and he had almost seven, so he beat the average. I made a table of his hospital visits from Amma's file. There were fourteen.
Everyone at home keeps crying in the kitchen. Amma calls me her brave boy. I don't really get why I'm not crying. I just feel like I need to understand it properly first.
Anyway, how are your exams going?
Pranav
P.S. Yesterday I found his reading glasses in my geometry box. He must have left them when he helped me with circles. I had to go and sit in the bathroom for a while. Not sure why I'm telling you this.

qa.q: How many hospital visits did Pranav count in his table?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: Why does Pranav feel he needs to understand the heart failure 'properly first'?
qa.a: Understanding makes the loss feel manageable and far away; the reading glasses in the geometry box show the sadness is already there underneath.

qa.q: What could Vidya write back that would help Pranav most?
qa.a: Vidya could thank him for the P.S., share a memory of Thatha, and say gently that tears can come later, instead of replying to the statistics.

qa.q: What might the family crying in the kitchen think about Pranav's calm?
qa.a: They might worry he is shut down or doesn't feel it, not seeing that the table and the facts are his way of holding the grief away for now.

grounding: A teenager emails a cousin about his grandfather's heart failure in facts and numbers, and only a postscript shows the grief breaking through.

passage:
"Deepak, you've hardly said a word since the funeral."
Okay, Mahima, you asked, so. It was a pulmonary embolism. A clot, from his leg, that went up into his lung. I read that it can happen after long bed rest, and Nanu had been in bed three weeks after his knee operation. The ambulance took eleven minutes. His oxygen was in the low eighties when they got there. I looked up every term that night.
Why are you looking at me like that? I'm fine. I'm just saying what happened. Mum keeps crying in the kitchen and I keep reading. It makes more sense to me this way.
Only thing is, his reading glasses are still on the arm of the sofa, and I can't pick them up. I don't know why. I keep walking round them.
Anyway. The ambulance time matters a lot, apparently.

qa.q: How long had Nanu been in bed after his knee operation?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: Why does it make more sense to Deepak to talk in medical terms?
qa.a: Deepak feels safer with facts about the clot and the ambulance; they keep the grief of losing Nanu at a distance while the family cries around Deepak.

qa.q: What moment could become a turning point for Deepak's grief?
qa.a: The reading glasses on the sofa that Deepak keeps walking round; if Mahima gently asks about them, or they sit near them together, the feeling might finally have room to come out.

qa.q: What might Mahima be thinking as Deepak lists oxygen levels in such an even way?
qa.a: Mahima is probably worried, sensing that the calm facts are covering real sadness, and unsure whether to push or just stay close.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose grandfather has died reciting medical details and numbers, keeping grief at arm's length, with the unpicked-up glasses hinting that tears will come later.

passage:
I'm Jatin, Ramesh's cousin. I came to Bareilly for our Dadi's thirteenth-day prayers, and all week Ramesh was the calmest person in the house.
Whenever a relative arrived, he explained it like a news report. "Her heart stopped at 4:10 a.m. The doctor said it was a cardiac arrest, not a heart attack; they're different things. They tried for twenty-five minutes." He even corrected Bua when she mixed up the names of Dadi's tablets. His voice stayed flat, as if he were reading from a page.
The aunties whispered that he was very mature. I wasn't sure. He was sixteen, and Dadi had packed his tiffin every single school day of his life.
On the last night I went up to the terrace and found him sitting beside her folded shawl, shoulders shaking. I sat down next to him and didn't say anything.

qa.q: Where did Jatin find Ramesh on the last night?
qa.a: On the terrace, sitting beside Dadi's folded shawl, shoulders shaking.

qa.q: Why might explaining the death like a news report feel safer to Ramesh?
qa.a: Precise facts give him something steady to hold while the loss is too big to feel; staying in the details keeps the pain of losing the Dadi who packed his tiffin at arm's length.

qa.q: What choice did Jatin make on the terrace, and why did it help?
qa.a: Jatin sat beside Ramesh without saying anything, giving the tears room instead of praising the calm or asking more questions.

qa.q: Why might the aunties and Jatin read Ramesh's calm so differently?
qa.a: The aunties took the flat voice as maturity, while Jatin knew how close Ramesh was to Dadi and sensed the calm might be holding grief back.

grounding: Illustrates, through a cousin's eyes, a teenager reciting medical facts about his grandmother's death in a flat voice, with the tears coming only later.
